text: An ancient knife, a doctor's blood, and an appetite that arrives by infection rather than by curse. That single change of cause does most of the work: Bill Gunn's 1973 film has on its hands not a monster out of folklore but a man of medicine with a condition he can name and cannot treat. Horror that year wanted speed. This takes a hundred and thirteen minutes, and the title sets a second name beside the doctor's, which suggests a film content to stay inside domestic rooms rather than prowl outside them. Its genre listing puts drama ahead of horror, and that order reads less like a cataloguing habit than an accurate account of where the weight falls — on hunger as something a person must go on living beside rather than something that hunts. The National Film Registry has since taken it in.

Made in 1942, about an occupation still under way while the cameras turned. A British bomber crew comes down in Holland with no aircraft, no Dutch, and no route home except through people who did not ask for them. Michael Powell strips the airmen of the machine that made them competent and leaves them a walking problem in arithmetic: how many strangers have to be told, how many of those can be trusted, how long a household can carry a secret of that size. The civilians hold the initiative throughout, which is unusual in a wartime picture built partly to steady the country paying for it. An Academy Award went to the screenplay, and that is the right prize — the danger sits in who says what to whom, in kitchens and back rooms where one wrong sentence ends several lives.

Fourteen minutes, two worlds, one commodity, and a price that moves in the first world and is felt in the second. A man decides on a whim to buy up the wheat of the earth; the cost of bread doubles; the people who grew the grain end up in charity lines. D.W. Griffith builds the thing out of alternation, cutting between the field and the men who trade what the field produced until the link requires no explaining. The farmers get wide, patient frames of labour. The buyer gets crowds and hurry. This is 1909, and the cross-cut is being put to work not to speed a rescue along but to lodge a complaint: the two halves are kept from meeting, and that separation is the argument. The National Film Registry keeps it. It is short enough to watch twice, which is roughly what its coldness requires.

The order is to blow a bridge in the Philippines and then stop the Japanese from rebuilding it, and no relief is coming. Tay Garnett films that assignment as a siege: fixed ground, shrinking supplies, an enemy that keeps returning to the same span. The squad is drawn from across the country and across its divisions, thrown together by an emergency with no interest in them as individuals. Hunger and sickness do as much damage as gunfire. What makes it odd as a 1943 studio release is the candour about arithmetic — these men exist to buy a general a few days, and the film says so rather than promising anyone a rescue. 114 minutes of holding ground that has already been written off. Whatever reassurance a wartime audience took from this, it was of a severe kind.

A fire station at rest, then horses, then a street taken at speed. Seven minutes was a substantial length in 1903, and Edwin S. Porter spends it on something that sounds elementary now and was not: making separate shots read as a single continuous event. The alarm sounds in one place and is answered in another; the horse-drawn pumper leaves the station and arrives at the fire; a window becomes a way in. Everything depends on an audience accepting that the horses in the second shot are the horses from the first, and on Porter arranging matters so that the acceptance is automatic. The camera does not move. The drama is in the joins. What survives best, past the technique, is the plain pleasure of the equipment going about work that was, at the time, simply work.

A planet is found to be on course to strike the Earth, and the response is to fly out and meet it. Flash Gordon runs 245 minutes, which is not a film's length but a serial's — instalments built to break off at the worst moment and resume a week later. The National Film Registry keeps a copy. Seen straight through, the machinery shows: the recaps, the escapes that have to be survivable, a tyrant named Ming who cannot be beaten early because there are chapters still to fill. Ray Taylor holds the pace the form pays for. What lasts is the confidence of the invention — a hostile planet, a despot, a scientist, and Dale, the best girl along for the ride, each sketched in a few strokes and asked to carry hours. In 1936, outer space was still cheap to build.

The film a man said he was making and the film he came home with are two different things, and Ross McElwee kept both. The announced project was General Sherman's route through the South and what remains where he burned it. What got shot is McElwee walking the same geography with a camera on his shoulder, filming the women who enter and leave his life, narrating dreams of nuclear holocaust in a voice that never lifts. Burt Reynolds turns up. The camera is simultaneously his method and his problem: people arrange themselves for it, he shelters behind it, and the history he abandoned keeps appearing anyway in the land and the families he passes through on the way to another date. Sundance gave it the documentary jury prize. At 158 minutes, the evasion has time to become the subject.

A boy of nearly nineteen wants the sea, and everything on shore has already been arranged for him. His father owns a café on the Marseille waterfront and has planned a life to match it; Fanny, who grew up beside him, picks the night before a five-year voyage to say what she has been holding. Joshua Logan spends 133 minutes on a situation that could be settled in ten, and the length is the point — these are people who talk around a decision because whoever makes it pays for it. The harbour does much of the work, all loading and water and the ordinary traffic of a town whose business is departure, and the film's Academy Award for colour cinematography was earned there. What keeps it from sentiment is the arithmetic underneath: neither choice available is a mistake, and both are irreversible.

A palace built on a Hollywood lot in black and white, and inside it an Englishwoman with a contract and a firm set of opinions. The story is set in 1862; the film was made in 1946, and the two dates press on each other in every scene where a woman from London explains something to a king who hired her precisely so that he would hear it. Whatever it knows of Siam it knows from books and set dressing — its Academy Award for black-and-white art direction is, in the end, a prize for persuasive plaster. What it does have is a real subject: two people of very unequal power conducting a long argument disguised as employment, each giving ground by inches. John Cromwell keeps the register conversational and lets the friendship take its time, because the interest lies in the negotiating.

Ten thousand dollars, lifted on impulse from the charity she chairs, and no way to replace it before someone counts. Cecil B. DeMille gets from a spending habit to a loan in very little time — the whole thing runs under an hour — and the loan is arranged with an ivory trader whose terms are never written down and never need to be. The film plays that arrangement as intimacy rather than commerce, which is where its charge comes from and also where its trouble lies: the fascination it directs at the lender is inseparable from the dread, and 1915 supplies no distance from either. The wife is granted no alibi. She is vain, careless, and cornered by arithmetic she began herself, and the camera watches her calculate. Held by the National Film Registry, and uncomfortable on more than one count.

The man has a serial number where a name should be, and the film treats that as ordinary. Fifteen minutes, shot at a university in 1967 by a student with access to equipment and no obligation to explain himself: George Lucas turns a chase through underground passages and sealed rooms into something nearer a readout than a story. The hunt is run by machines — computers, cameras, a system watching a man become a set of coordinates — and the pursuers are mostly people looking at screens. Exposition is refused outright. What carries it is rhythm, and the flat courtesy of an institution addressing a number. The National Film Registry admitted a student exercise, which is not common, and the reason declares itself in the first minute: this is a future administered rather than ruled, and the difference is where the fear sits.

Chalk will not hold a garden; the soil is too thin, and whatever is planted in it fails quietly. That is also the condition of the house on the English south coast where Ronald Neame's film takes place, and of the girl growing up inside it, who has frightened off one governess after another. The next applicant arrives with references nobody can check. The mystery promised by the genre listing turns out to be a withheld biography rather than a crime, and the film keeps its secret in plain sight while the household discusses planting and manners. Edith Evans plays the grandmother who raised the granddaughter and let the garden go. An Academy Award for supporting actress came out of it. Almost everything happens indoors, in rooms where people are courteous and nothing is confessed.

Two strangers in a crowded city get a single day off, and the crowd is at least as much the subject as they are. Pál Fejős made Lonesome in 1928, at the far end of the silent era's technical confidence, and he spends that confidence on ordinary things: getting up, going to work, riding out to the amusement park along with everyone else in town. The romance is nearly incidental to the traffic. Seventy minutes leaves no room for a subplot, so the film follows two people through a holiday afternoon and lets the machinery of pleasure — the rides, the beach, the press of bodies — decide how near they can get. Then it separates them in a crowd, which the same machinery makes easy. The National Film Registry holds it. It is unusually interested in what a day off actually gives and takes back.

He marries a nurse for her savings and her competence at the operating table, and he knows exactly what he is doing, which somehow makes it worse. Lucas Marsh intends to be a first-class doctor rather than a successful one, and that distinction excuses a great deal in his own accounting. Stanley Kramer takes 135 minutes over the domestic consequences: a practice in a small town, a household funded by another person's years of thrift, a wife glad to be useful and not asked for more. It won an Academy Award for sound, which in a film so full of hospital procedure is not a trivial credit. The real subject is an assumption — that a man holding himself to a high standard owes nothing to whoever supplies the means. Then a woman in town takes an interest, and the arrangement starts to show its limits.
